mechanism.text: The first shot fixes which side is frame left and which frame right, and fixes the directions of attention across the film space; staying on one side of the line preserves both.

item.visible_content: Two figures, two pages apart, shot at the same waterfront location with the same two actors in the same wardrobe and the same framing scale. Figure 5.4 (correct) pairs three overhead diagrams with three frames: D a wide two-shot, E character A at frame left looking frame right, F character B right of centre looking frame LEFT. Figure 5.5 (incorrect) reuses frames D and E unchanged and replaces F with the same actor now placed at frame LEFT looking frame RIGHT. The third diagram in 5.5 carries the drawn label "WRONG SIDE OF LINE".

source_terms: By keeping the camera essentially in the same place, and moving the actors, you can capture all the motion and emotion of the scene without any complex moves.
you need to block the actors' movements so that the character who is doing most of the talking faces the camera
item.claim: Technique 8.7. For an argument, hold a wide master with almost no camera movement and let the actors circle and pace, blocked so that whoever is dominating the scene faces the camera and the turn has already happened before the other begins to dominate. The source states the standing problem — one actor is always facing away — and requires that actor to be given enough body acting to keep a presence. It also gives a fallback: if no take is perfect, shoot coverage that need not be faces, since hands and feet will enable a cut while keeping the focus on the argument's energy.

mechanism.text: People arguing circle and pace, so the movement the scene needs is already there; making the actors carry it keeps the audience oriented in a way a moving camera would not.

scope.conditions: arguments and other scenes with continuous movement between two people

caveats.text: the only technique in the chapter that solves the chapter's problem without moving the camera at all, and the only one that ends by planning for a cut

item.rationale: The executable content of all seven techniques: where the camera goes, where the actors go, in what order, and how the two are timed against each other. source_terms: how do you move from one place to the other without it seeming forced?

item.claim: The chapter's organising problem, stated in its first technique and recurring in every one after it: how to move the audience's attention from one part of a scene to another without cutting and without the move seeming arbitrary. The source's general answer is to hide the camera's movement behind something happening in the scene, and it treats the cut as the default that the techniques exist to improve on.
item.interpretation_basis: The source never states a chapter-level thesis. Each of the seven techniques poses its own problem and gives its own solution. Reading them as seven answers to one question — how to redirect attention without a cut — is ours, and the evidence for it is that six of the seven explicitly contrast their method with cutting or panning, and the chapter is titled Directing Attention.

scope.conditions: scenes with more than one point of interest

caveats.text: the source does not argue that continuous shots are better than cutting in general; it says cutting is fine but less flowing, and one technique ends by recommending a cut

source_stated_problems: moving from one place to the other with it seeming forced
source_stated_remedies: camouflage the camera movement behind an action

item.claim: Technique 8.2. In a busy scene the camera backs off as one character advances, as if making room for her, and the space this opens brings a second character into focus. The whole scene plays in one shot. The stated requirements are that the characters be moving and that their movement be motivated — fetching a file, not wandering — and the stated result is that the audience feels no camera move at all, only a change of subject.

item.source_title: Timothy Samara, Making and Breaking the Grid: A Graphic Design Layout Workshop, 2nd ed. (Rockport Publishers, 2017)
item.source_locator: Ch. 2 'Breaking the Grid', Alternative Architectures — Centered-Axis Structure (spine 6)
item.question: A centred layout for a cultural institution has been criticised as inert. Samara predicts this failure. What does he say causes it, and what are his remedies — noting which dimension the remedies are allowed to touch?
item.answer: He says symmetry is unforgiving with regard to layout flexibility because it demands that every element adhere to a single axis, and elements that do not typically appear disunified from the whole. The resulting restfulness and uniformity are problematic relative to the goals of designed communication: a viewer is likely to gloss over the material and come to an intellectual rest quickly rather than investigate the work more intently. His remedies all work on the dimensions symmetry does not govern, because moving elements off the axis is precisely what is unavailable. Exaggerate contrasts in scale or proportion and in spacing, density and rhythm. Enlarge the symmetrically organised forms until they are clearly bigger than the remaining symmetrical spaces, so their confrontation with the format becomes tense and the static quality is reduced. Juxtapose dramatically different emphases in proportion, among both the forms and the spaces between them, under a defined logic of progression or alternation along the axis. And make radical changes in size or in lightness and darkness so that lateral movement is reordered as movement from near to far.
item.support: "Centered-Axis Structure": symmetry unforgiving, elements off-axis appear disunified, viewer comes to intellectual rest quickly; exaggerating contrasts in scale and spacing as critical to optical vitality; oversized forms creating tension with the format; a logic of progression along the axis; radical size and value changes reordering movement dimensionally.
confounders: recommending that elements be moved off the axis, which is the one repair symmetry forecloses
assuming restfulness is the goal of a symmetrical layout; Samara treats it as the problem
reaching for colour variety in general — his named levers are scale, spacing/density, and lightness/darkness

source_terms: A two-shot will establish frame left and frame right, therefore also establishing screen direction, look room, and lines of attention for the two characters.
Clearly, with both persons looking right, they would appear to be talking to some third, but unseen, person off-screen.
item.claim: The action line exists for people as well as movement. A two-shot fixes which character is frame left and which frame right, and with that the screen direction, the look room and each character's line of attention. Every coverage single must keep the characters on their established sides looking in their established directions. If one single is shot from the far side of the line, both characters appear to look the same way, so they read as addressing an unseen third person — which makes no sense to an audience who can account for only two.

mechanism.text: The audience reconstructs the geometry of the space from the direction each character faces. Two characters facing the same way cannot be facing each other, so the audience infers a third party rather than a mistake.

caveats.text: the source states the requirement absolutely: both shots must come from the initial side of the arc, never one from each

they would appear to be talking to some third, but unseen, person off-screen

source_terms: Screen direction is the movement of talent or objects toward frame right or frame left. This must be maintained as you transition from one shot to the next
item.claim: Screen direction — whether talent or objects move toward frame left or frame right — must hold across a cut whenever the next shot continues the same movement. Where the available shot contradicts the established direction, the editor must insert a shot that continues the narrative and breaks the audience's attention on the direction of travel.

source_terms: the cut-away is any brief shot that will provide the appropriate distraction and time filler to allow the audience to make the leap in logic
item.claim: Inserting any brief shot between two mismatched shots gives the audience both a distraction and enough elapsed time to accept that the change happened off screen. The same device is named twice in the chapter: as a cut-away for an object or action mismatch, and as an insert shot for a reversal of screen direction.

mechanism.text: The intervening shot breaks the audience's continuous attention on the mismatched element and supplies the screen time in which the change could plausibly have occurred.

caveats.text: the source requires only that the inserted shot be logical and fit the narrative flow; it sets no minimum duration and no test for whether the break was long enough

source_terms: you use the alternate placement of characters frame left and frame right to generate interest

item.claim: The editor cannot compose the shots but chooses which compositions meet at a cut. Placing one character at frame left with open look room to the right, and cutting to a matching shot of the other character at frame right with look room to the left, makes the viewer's gaze travel across the screen at the cut and land on the new face. The source calls this eye-line match or eye trace and likens the effect to a tennis ball crossing a court.

mechanism.text: While watching character A at frame left the viewer is aware that A's attention is directed across the screen to the right. At the cut the viewer traces that eye-line across the empty look room and is rewarded by finding character B where the trace ended.

scope.conditions: two-person dialogue coverage with matching reciprocal singles

caveats.text: the source stresses that the placement of character B must match the eye-line from character A for the reward to occur
the mechanism is asserted about where viewers look; no eye-tracking or other measurement is offered

source_terms: These reaction shots should be shown to help break up the continual, verbal assault of the one character and to provide new information about the listening party
item.claim: A long monologue delivered to another person should still be cut visually. The listener will react facially or bodily, and showing those reactions both breaks up the continuous speech and supplies new information about the listener. The exception is a character talking to himself with no reason to reference other shots, where the monologue may stand unedited.

caveats.text: the justification is the information rule, so the reaction shot qualifies as an edit for the same reason any shot does; the source does not treat it as a special licence
